candidates.statement: I. Introduction 14 The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is issuing this draft guidance document to describe 15 relevant information that should be provided in a premarket submission (i.e., premarket approval 16 (PMA) applications, humanitarian device exemption (HDE) applications, premarket notification 17 (510(k)) submissions, investigational device exemption (IDE) applications and De Novo 18 requests) to support the evaluation of thermal effects of medical devices that produce local, 19 regional, and/or systemic changes in tissue temperature (i.e., heating and/or cooling) due to their 20 use. The recommendations in this guidance reflect current review practices and are intended to 21 promote consistency and facilitate efficient review of thermal effects data for these devices. 22 Where available, device-specific guidance documents and/or standards may include additional 23 technical recommendations on thermal effects evaluation that should be considered. 24

candidates.statement: Experimental Assessment of Tissue Effects and Thermal 88 Energy Spread 89 (1) Experimental Models Experimental assessment of tissue effects and thermal energy spread can be conducted using 91 phantoms, ex vivo animal tissue models, and/or in vivo animal testing, as applicable to the 92 intended use. The suitability of each method for a given device depends on the magnitude and 93 distribution of the heating and/or cooling, as well as the availability of appropriate experimental 94 models. For example, tissue temperature changes may be local (confined to a small volume of tissue or a portion of a specific anatomical structure), regional (affecting the majority or all of a 96 given anatomical structure and potentially one or more immediately surrounding structures), or 97 systemic (affecting multiple diffuse anatomical structures or all body). While it may be feasible 98 to develop a suitable phantom model or ex vivo animal tissue model for devices with local tissue 99 temperature changes, it may be more challenging to do so for devices with regional or systemic effects, where the impact of blood flow on the development of tissue effects would need to be 101 accounted for. 102

candidates.statement: 245 b. Test Methods Tissue effects are a function of spatial temperature distribution over time (i.e., “temperature-time 246 history”), which involves temperature change (i.e., heating or cooling) as well as returning of the 247 temperature to baseline value. Therefore, testing should be performed such that the tissue is 248 exposed to the minimum, average, and worst-case temperature-time history. The tissue should be 249 maintained at the baseline temperature relevant for the indications for use (e.g., core body 250 temperature for internal tissues) prior to application of the device. After application of the 251 device, the tissue should be allowed to return to the baseline temperature as it would under 252 clinical conditions of use and energy flow in order for the tissue effects to fully develop. Some 253 tissue effects may take hours to days, or longer in some cases, to fully evolve after the thermal 254 exposure. For example, assessment of electroporation-induced lesions should take into account 255 that the full extent of tissue damage may not be evident immediately after the electroporation 256 procedure, and visible fibrotic lesions may take days or weeks to form. For questions regarding 257 specific time points to study a tissue effect, we recommend you submit a Pre-Submission to 258 obtain early feedback. 3

Assessing Thermally Affected Tissue Region 310 For ex vivo tissue testing and in vivo animal testing, you should provide an assessment of the 311 thermally affected tissue region and related thermal energy spread. The thermally affected tissue 312 region is the size (i.e., length, width, depth, and volume) of tissue with damage and/or adverse 313 effects resulting from device use. The related thermal energy spread is determined by measuring 314 the temperature-time history, or the spatial temperature distribution over time. Recommended 315

candidates.statement: 468 Clinical data may be needed when results from non-clinical and animal thermal effects evaluation studies are found insufficient to support the safety and effectiveness of the device 469 when used as intended. Clinical studies should be designed to test the full range of device 470 parameters and proposed conditions of use in the intended patient population. The study design 471 should include safety measures to provide reasonable assurance of safety of subjects undergoing 472 the study. The results should include a complete account of the thermally affected tissue regions 473 including, but not limited to, thermal injury to vital structures, skin burns (if applicable), as well 474 as the corresponding temperature-time history depicting the thermal energy spread, including 475 real-time temperature monitoring of target and non-target critical organs. 476
candidates.context: IV. Labeling 478 In addition to labeling requirements and recommendations from any relevant regulations or 479 statute, and device-specific guidances, we recommend that you include a chart and/or graph in 480 your labeling that provides the dimensions (i.e., length, width, depth, and volume) of the 481 thermally affected tissue region in relation to the power setting, and duration of activation for 482 different tissue types. This information is important to inform users of the expected damage and 483 to facilitate safe use. 484
